To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

estrogen receptor immunoreactive neurons are present in the organum vascularosum of the laminae terminalis, the anteroventral preoptic nucleus, the medial preoptic nucleus and the nucleus tractus Solitarii.

the supraoptic nucleus receives a substantial number of estrogen receptor-containing afferents from the organum vasculum of the laminae terminalis (OVLT), anteroventral and preoptic areas, and brainstem.

estrogen receptor-immunopositive neurons project to the supraoptic and paraventricular magnocellular nuclei in the rat, and that these estrogen receptor-positive neurons originate from the organum vasculosum of the laminae terminalis, the preoptic area, the median preoptic area, and the brainstem.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of estrogen in modulating the activity of magneto- and parvocellular neurons in hypothalamus and brainstem that regulate the secretion of oxytocin and/or vasopressin and the activity of the autonomic nervous system in modulating cardiovascular, renal and reproductive function.
the neuroendocrine control of the hypothalamos-pituitary-adrenal and -gonadotrophin axes.
the neurochemical basis of the effects of estrogen on magnocellular oxytoic and vasopressic neurons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the supraoptic nucleus receives estrogen-receptive inputs from the lamina terminali, anteroventrolateral preoptic area and the ventrolateral division ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus.
estrogen may influence the activity of the supraoptic nucleus in an indirect manner, via the first-order neurons that project to this nucleus.
the first-order neurons to the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei are estrogen receptive and that estrogen may modulate magnocellular activity by acting on first-order neurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the supraoptic nucleus is an estrogen-responsive structure.

estrogen may regulate magnocellular oxytotcin and vasopressine neurons indirectly via estrogen-receptive first-order neurons projecting from the organum vasculum lamina terminalis to the supraoptic nuclei.

estrogen may influence the electrical and/or biosynthetic activity (i.e. vasopressin and oxytocin release) of magnocellular neurons by acting on estrogen receptor-containing neurons that project to the supraoptic magnocellular neurons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
estrogen receptor immunoreactive cells are present in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, but they do not appear to be vasopressin- and/or oxytocin-expressing neurons.
the brain has a lot of estrogen receptor neurons that are not in the hypothalamus and are not in the pituitary.

estrogen receptors are present in neurons of the lamina terminals and the medial preoptic area, which project to the magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic nucleus, and these neurons may play an important role in estrogen regulation of magnocellular neurons.
